text: About 2,300 years ago, Tamil-speaking people lived in the far south of India, in a land called Tamilakam.
src: Sangam-age Tamilakam was the ancient Tamil-speaking country of southern India / Usually c. 300 BCE–300 CE

text: Three families of kings ruled it: the Cheras, the Cholas and the Pandyas.
They often fought one another to be the strongest.
src: Between 300 BCE and 300 CE Tamilakam was ruled by three dynasties, the Pandya, Chola and Chera
The three dynasties often competed for supremacy, and the poems record their conflicts

text: Most people were farmers, who grew rice, pepper, sugarcane and millet.
Others wove cotton and silk cloth, fished for pearls or built ships.
src: Agriculture was the main occupation / Paddy was the staple / pepper, sugarcane and millets were also grown
weaving, pearl fishing, smithing and shipbuilding were the chief crafts, with cotton and silk cloth

text: Ships carried their pearls, pepper and cloth across the sea as far as Rome.
Roman coins and jars have been found in their land.
src: a sea trade in pearls, pepper and textiles that brought Roman coins to Kerala and Tamil Nadu / traded overseas as far as Rome
Roman coins and amphorae found in Kerala and Tamil Nadu confirm the trade

text: People of several faiths, Hindus, Jains and Buddhists, lived side by side.
The poems call Murugan, a young god seated on a blue peacock, “the favoured god of the Tamils”.
src: Several faiths lived side by side. / Hinduism, in the forms of Vaishnavism, Kaumaram, Shaktism, Shaivism and Dravidian folk religion, together with Jainism and Buddhism, was present in the Tamil country
is Murugan, praised in the poems as “the favoured god of the Tamils”, ever young and seated on a blue peacock

text: Their 473 poets, at least 27 of them women, left 2,381 poems of love and war.
The palm-leaf books were forgotten for centuries, until scholars found and printed them more than 130 years ago.
src: Its 2,381 surviving poems by 473 poets, at least 27 of them women, sing of love and war
The Sangam poems were forgotten for much of the second millennium / in 1883 U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar found a major store of their palm-leaf manuscripts / together they printed more than 100 works
